382.t: Who influenced her and whether anyone imitated her
382.s: She says nobody identified her style with anyone, citing Adelaide Hall and wordless vocals with Ellington.
382.q: Well I don't think that they knew what was happening at the time. Nobody does the things that I -- nobody sing them. I've heard orchestrations, and I've heard male singers do it -- do like some of the things that I'm doing now on my current repertoire. But of the females, I don't hear them doing…

382.t: Dinah Shore and Peggy Lee as listeners of her style
382.s: Dinah Shore acknowledged her as a major influence; Peggy Lee also mentioned her; she was influenced by Ella, Billie and Ethel Waters.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: Dinah Shore? I'm not too sure. Dinah came along at the same time that I did. I have a feeling that there was a group of singers that came along at the same time I did who were probably coached along the lines that I would be singing, you know. They probably were told to and maybe they listened to…

382.t: Mildred Bailey's warning and Midge Williams
382.s: Mildred Bailey advised her on style so she wouldn't be a second Ella; Midge Williams was more commercial.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: You know, I remember very vividly when I first came to New York, Mildred Bailey was popular. And she was among the musicians, you know, that used to come in because she was probably with Kurby and Buster and Red, you know, they were all together. And I had the audacity to approach Mildred Bailey…

667.t: Singers who influenced Jackie, especially Sarah Vaughan
667.s: Everything is an influence; Ella, Billie, Peggy Lee, Sarah Vaughan, and finding her own sound by serving the song.
667.q: I don’t know what all, the funny songs you know, can’t remember even the rest. That was before I sang “Happiness is a Thing Called Joe” after I heard Frances Wayne sing it. But you know when people say who were your influences, everything you hear is your influence you know? I mean there were so…

668.t: Influence, imitation, and Armstrong versus Parker followers
668.s: Davern says strong stylists may have no followers; Armstrong's followers sounded different while Parker's sounded like him; he criticizes clones and mentions Ethel Waters.
668.q: Yeah, but the thing is this, Mike, I mean let’s put it this way. There are people who have very strong — if you’re stylistically strong, there’s a very good possibility you may have no followers and influence no one because you’re unique in that way. I mean unless you are truly a revolutionary, vis…

669.t: Guitar icons: Wes Montgomery, Burrell, Martino, Benson
669.s: He names Wes Montgomery, Kenny Burrell, Pat Martino and George Benson, and says he is influenced by pianists, saxophonists and trumpeters.
669.ch: Learning from masters and guitar ideas
669.q: Well when I came up, the first one like I said the first one I was listening to was Wes Montgomery and then from there I listened to Kenny Burrell and from there there was Pat Martino and then in the 70s I finally got some records by George Benson and I heard him and I said, “Oh, no!” But after a…

670.t: Mother's pride and meeting Billie Holiday
670.s: She met Holiday several times, including when Holiday came to hear her at the Onyx, and explains how singers move from their idol's influence to their own style.
670.q: I met her at least three times. Once in Chicago she was leaving after one of the shows, a break, probably going somewhere to eat, and they introduced me to her, and I was just in heaven, and she had this big white fox fur on, and a big flower. Oh she was so beautiful, and my heart almost stopped…

671.s: Twenty-five dollars a night with Eckstine playing lead alto, a few solos per band, and influences Hodges, Carter and Willie Smith.
671.q: Well with Billy Eckstine I think I made more than I’d ever made, I made twenty-five dollars a night. Worked almost every night.

672.t: Influences: Lena Horne, Dinah Washington, Little Jimmy Scott
672.s: She names where her gowns, humor and phrasing came from.
672.q: No. Because I don’t – if you notice, I haven’t mentioned any singers except Al Hibbler. I didn’t really get to see female singers. I didn’t really see what they did, other than to know that Lena Horne was Lena Horne and to hear the humor in Dinah Washington’s records. I was already signed with…

566.t: Sounding like Billie Holiday, Mildred Bailey and Ella
566.s: People say she sounds like Billie, Mildred Bailey or Ella. Dance notes Stanley Dance's point that Humes's early blues records were compared to Mildred before Bailey had recorded.
566.q: People have said I sound like Billie Holiday, I sound like Mildred Bailey, and some of them say I sound like Ella. And I said, that's nice.

95.t: Where her blues style came from; hearing Mamie Smith records
95.s: She says she got her blues from within and from Mamie Smith records heard from her porch; people told her she sounded like Bessie Smith.
95.q: No, (unintelligible) I got that from my own blues. (Unintelligible) I guess I really was a blues singer (unintelligible).
